answer:
**Optimizers differ in what they remember about previous gradients.** SGD uses the current gradient. Momentum retains a decayed direction, helping consistent progress through noisy updates. Nesterov momentum modifies how the look-ahead correction is formed. RMSProp tracks squared gradients to scale coordinates, while Adam tracks both first and second moments. AdamW separates weight decay from Adam's adaptive gradient transformation. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

**A landscape intuition.** In a narrow valley, gradients may alternate strongly across the steep direction while pointing consistently along the valley. Momentum can cancel some alternating motion and accumulate the consistent component. Adaptive scaling can reduce steps in coordinates with historically large gradients, though that history is only an imperfect guide to current curvature.

No optimizer removes the need for a suitable learning rate, initialization, batch strategy, and loss definition. Adam's extra state consumes memory; SGD is simpler but can require more careful tuning in some settings. Different epsilon and momentum conventions can also make apparently identical configurations differ.

Compare matched training budgets and tune each optimizer fairly. A result where Adam uses its tuned learning rate and SGD uses an arbitrary one says little about their intrinsic tradeoff. Record parameter groups, weight-decay exclusions, scheduler behavior, and state restoration so the experiment is reproducible.

**Technical details and references.**

SGD moves against the current gradient; momentum averages a velocity to reduce oscillation and accelerate consistent directions. Nesterov momentum evaluates or approximates the gradient at a look-ahead point. RMSProp divides by a running root mean square of gradients. Adam combines first and second moments with bias correction. AdamW decouples parameter decay from those moments. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101)

$$m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\quad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2,\quad \theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon}.$$

Adaptive methods handle coordinate-scale differences but require extra state. SGD's lower state cost and different implicit bias can be useful. Compare tuned schedules, regularization, compute, and validation performance; optimizer names alone do not determine quality.
